stem: The meeting was cancelled because the manager was ill.
options: The manager's illness led to the cancellation of the meeting.
The manager became ill during the meeting.
The meeting was held without the manager, who was ill.
The manager cancelled the meeting and then became ill.
solutionSteps: Identify the causal direction: illness caused the cancellation.
Check the order of events: he was ill first, then the meeting was cancelled.
Option 1 preserves both the cause and the order.

trapExplanations.1: Places the illness during the meeting, but the original says the meeting never happened.
trapExplanations.2: Says the meeting took place, contradicting 'was cancelled'.
trapExplanations.3: Reverses the order — the original makes illness the cause, not the consequence.

stem: Few students passed the exam on their first attempt.
options: Most students needed more than one attempt to pass the exam.
No student passed the exam on the first attempt.
Most students passed the exam on their first attempt.
The exam could only be taken once.
solutionSteps: 'Few' means a small number, but not zero.
If few passed first time, the majority did not — they needed another attempt.
Option 1 states exactly that.

trapExplanations.1: 'Few' is not 'none' — some students did pass. This is the classic quantifier trap.
trapExplanations.3: Adds a rule about retakes that the original never mentions.

stem: Unless you register by Friday, you will not be able to attend the workshop.
options: Registering by Friday is required in order to attend the workshop.
If you register by Friday, you will definitely attend the workshop.
Registration closes after the workshop begins.
Everyone who attends the workshop registered on Friday.
solutionSteps: 'Unless X, not Y' means X is necessary for Y.
Necessary is not the same as sufficient — registering makes attendance possible, not certain.
Option 1 says 'required', which is exactly necessity.

trapExplanations.1: Turns a necessary condition into a sufficient one — 'definitely' overstates the original.
trapExplanations.2: Invents a timing detail that is not in the sentence.
trapExplanations.3: Says everyone registered exactly on Friday, but the original allows registering earlier.

stem: The proposal, while economically sound, was politically unacceptable.
options: The proposal made economic sense but could not be accepted politically.
The proposal was rejected because it was economically weak.
The proposal was acceptable both economically and politically.
Politicians agreed with the proposal despite its economic flaws.
solutionSteps: 'While X, Y' sets up a concession: X is granted, Y is the problem.
X = economically sound (positive), Y = politically unacceptable (negative).
Option 1 keeps both halves with the same polarity.

trapExplanations.1: Reverses the economics — the original grants that it was sound.
trapExplanations.3: Inverts both halves: politicians agreeing, economics flawed.

stem: Not all of the allegations were substantiated.
options: Some of the allegations were not supported by evidence.
None of the allegations were supported by evidence.
All of the allegations were false.
The allegations were all proven true.
solutionSteps: 'Not all' negates the universal claim, leaving a partial one.
It means at least one was unsubstantiated — but not necessarily all.
Option 1 says 'some ... not', which is exactly the negation of 'all'.

trapExplanations.1: 'Not all' is not 'none'. This is the single most common restatement trap on the test.
trapExplanations.2: Overstates in the same direction as option 1, and adds a falsity claim.

stem: The company only began investing in safety after the accident occurred.
options: Before the accident, the company had not invested in safety.
The accident happened because the company invested in safety.
The company invested in safety in order to prevent the accident.
The company stopped investing in safety once the accident occurred.
solutionSteps: 'Only began ... after X' places the start of the action strictly after X.
That entails nothing of the kind happened before X.
Option 1 states that entailment directly.

trapExplanations.1: Reverses cause and effect — the accident prompted the investment, not the other way round.
trapExplanations.2: Prevention would require investing before the accident, contradicting 'after'.
trapExplanations.3: Turns beginning into stopping — the opposite action.

stem: Her findings are significant not because they are surprising, but because they are so easily replicated.
options: The importance of her findings lies in their reproducibility rather than their novelty.
Her findings are both surprising and easy to replicate.
Her findings are unimportant because they are unsurprising.
Her findings would be more significant if they were surprising.
solutionSteps: 'Not because X, but because Y' rejects X as the reason and asserts Y.
X = surprising (novelty), Y = easily replicated (reproducibility).
Option 1 preserves the rejection of X and the assertion of Y.

trapExplanations.1: The original denies that the findings are surprising as the source of significance; this asserts both.
trapExplanations.2: The original affirms significance — this denies it.
trapExplanations.3: Introduces a hypothetical comparison the original never makes.

stem: Had the warning been issued earlier, the damage might have been contained.
options: The damage could possibly have been limited if the warning had come sooner.
The warning was issued early and the damage was contained.
The damage was certainly caused by the late warning.
An earlier warning would definitely have prevented all damage.
solutionSteps: 'Had X ...' is an unreal past conditional: X did not happen.
'Might have been' expresses possibility, not certainty.
Option 1 keeps both the counterfactual and the hedged possibility.

trapExplanations.1: States as fact what the original explicitly presents as contrary to fact.
trapExplanations.2: 'Certainly' overstates 'might' and turns possibility into established causation.
trapExplanations.3: 'Definitely ... all damage' doubly overstates: 'might' becomes certainty and 'contained' becomes total prevention.

stem: The regulation applies to all vehicles except those manufactured before 2010.
options: Vehicles made in 2010 or later are subject to the regulation.
Only vehicles manufactured before 2010 must follow the regulation.
The regulation applies to no vehicle manufactured after 2010.
All vehicles, regardless of age, must comply with the regulation.
solutionSteps: The rule covers everything, minus one carved-out group.
The carve-out is 'manufactured before 2010', so what remains is 2010 and later.
Option 1 describes precisely the remaining set.

trapExplanations.1: Inverts the exception — the pre-2010 vehicles are the ones excluded, not the only ones included.
trapExplanations.2: Also inverts the rule, exempting exactly the group that is covered.

stem: The shop opens at nine and closes at six.
options: The shop is open for nine hours each day.
The shop is open for six hours each day.
The shop opens at six and closes at nine.
The shop is closed between nine and six.
solutionSteps: Convert to a 24-hour span: nine in the morning to six in the evening.
From 9 to 18 is nine hours.
Option 1 states that duration.

trapExplanations.1: Takes the closing hour as the duration.
trapExplanations.3: Inverts open and closed — that is the period it is open.

stem: Everyone in the class except Maya finished the assignment.
options: Maya was the only one who did not finish.
Only Maya finished the assignment.
Nobody finished the assignment.
Maya finished before the others.
solutionSteps: 'Everyone except X' means all but X.
So the rest finished and X did not.
Option 1 states exactly that.

trapExplanations.1: Inverts the exception, making Maya the only finisher.
trapExplanations.3: Says Maya finished, which the exception denies.

options: He is usually late.
He is never late.
He always arrives on time.
He never arrives at all.
solutionSteps: 'Rarely' means seldom but not never.
If punctuality is rare, lateness is the norm.
'Usually late' preserves the frequency.

trapExplanations.2: Also the reverse of what is stated.
trapExplanations.3: 'Rarely on time' still means he arrives — just late.

stem: The policy was adopted despite strong opposition from the board.
options: The board objected, but the policy was adopted anyway.
The board's opposition prevented the policy.
The board supported the policy strongly.
The policy was adopted because the board objected.
solutionSteps: 'Despite X' concedes X and asserts the outcome anyway.
X is board opposition; the outcome is adoption.
Option 1 keeps both.

trapExplanations.1: 'Despite' means the opposition did not prevent it.
trapExplanations.3: Turns concession into causation — the opposition did not cause adoption.

stem: Sales rose in every region apart from the north, where they held steady.
options: Sales did not fall in any region.
Sales fell in the north.
Sales rose in every region including the north.
Sales rose only in the north.
solutionSteps: Everywhere but the north: rose. In the north: held steady.
Holding steady is neither a rise nor a fall.
So no region saw a decline.

trapExplanations.1: 'Held steady' explicitly rules out a fall. The most tempting misreading.
trapExplanations.2: Contradicts the exception for the north.

stem: No decision will be made before the report is published.
options: A decision can only come after publication of the report.
A decision will be made as soon as the report is published.
The report will be published after the decision.
No decision will ever be made.
solutionSteps: 'No X before Y' makes Y a prerequisite for X.
Publication must precede any decision.
It does not promise a decision will follow.

trapExplanations.1: Turns a necessary condition into a guarantee with a timetable.
trapExplanations.2: Reverses the order of the two events.
trapExplanations.3: The statement delays a decision, it does not rule one out.

stem: The treaty is binding on signatories only insofar as their domestic law permits.
options: Domestic law sets the limit of each signatory's obligation.
The treaty overrides the domestic law of signatories.
Signatories have no obligations under the treaty.
Domestic law must be changed to match the treaty.
solutionSteps: 'Only insofar as X permits' makes X the ceiling on the obligation.
X is domestic law.
So obligation extends exactly as far as domestic law allows, and no further.

trapExplanations.1: Exactly reverses the hierarchy the clause establishes.
trapExplanations.2: There are obligations — they are bounded, not absent.
trapExplanations.3: The clause accommodates domestic law rather than demanding it change.

stem: It is not that the method fails, but that its successes cannot be distinguished from chance.
options: The method may work, but the evidence cannot show that it does.
The method has been shown to fail.
The method succeeds more often than chance would predict.
The method works only by chance.
solutionSteps: 'Not that X, but that Y' denies X and asserts Y.
X is failure — denied. Y is indistinguishability from chance.
That is a claim about evidence, not about the method being wrong.

trapExplanations.1: Failure is precisely what the sentence denies.
trapExplanations.2: If successes exceeded chance they would be distinguishable — the opposite is stated.
trapExplanations.3: Asserts the method does not work, going beyond a claim about evidence. The strongest distractor.

stem: Far from settling the question, the new findings have multiplied the possible explanations.
options: The findings left the question more open than before.
The findings resolved the question conclusively.
The findings eliminated most competing explanations.
The findings confirmed the existing explanation.
solutionSteps: 'Far from X' asserts the opposite of X.
X is settling the question, so the question was not settled.
'Multiplied the explanations' means more openness, not less.

trapExplanations.2: Multiplying explanations is the opposite of eliminating them.
trapExplanations.3: Confirmation would reduce the range of explanations, not expand it.
